What I actually do

Three things, in some order, on almost every project.

Automations & workflows

Setting up the behind-the-scenes logic — GoHighLevel, Make.com, or straight inside the email platform — so the next step happens on its own.

List cleanup & segmentation

Going through a contact list, clearing out anyone who's gone quiet, and grouping the rest by what they actually care about.

Segment A Segment B Segment C

Signup forms & welcome flows

Building the form someone fills out and the automatic email they get right after, so nobody joins a list and hears nothing.

Email & signup work

The actual sends — what a subscriber opens in their inbox.

Campaign Monitor

Weekly newsletter

Built as a recurring template inside the email platform — same structure every send, new content dropped in each time. Goes out to a segmented slice of the list on a fixed schedule, so it never depends on someone remembering to hit send.

GoHighLevel

Campaign launch email

Set up as a one-off automated send triggered off the existing list, with the RSVP button tracked and a reminder queued behind it for anyone who clicked but didn't confirm.

Before the flow, after the flow

The same signup widget, on the same page — before any automation sat behind it, and after.

Before

Before the sequence went live: a signup widget sitting on the page, collecting nothing. 0 subscribers, 0 pop-ups shown, 0% conversion.

→
After
Best open rate Best CTOR

Once the welcome flow was live: that first email became the single best-performing send in the whole account — 93.52% open rate, 78.7% click rate, out of 108 sent.

For this client — a coach launching a free-ebook opt-in — I set a 24-hour delay before the next email in the sequence: long enough that the welcome email doesn't feel automatic, short enough that they still remember signing up. That pacing is most of why the open rate above holds up.

What building my own list taught me

A while back I built an email list from zero to launch a paid guide I'd written. No existing audience, no paid ads. Just a lead magnet, a signup form, and a plan to earn attention before asking for anything.

I mapped a five-week nurture sequence to move people from "just joined" to "ready to buy," then set the whole thing to run on its own. The list itself was never really the point. The system behind it was — the same cleanup, segmentation, and sequencing logic that turns a few thousand quiet contacts into a list that actually gets used.
